body_html:
A love letter in Spanish is one of the most romantic gifts you can give a Spanish-speaking partner. Spanish has a long tradition of love letters and poetry, and its vocabulary for feelings is rich and expressive. You don’t need perfect grammar: a sincere letter with a few mistakes will mean far more than a flawless one copied from the internet. This guide gives you the structure, the phrases and a full sample letter to help you write your own.

Key takeaways
  • Open with Querido/a, Mi amor or Mi vida.
  • Be specific: memories and details matter more than big words.
  • Use te quiero for warm love and te amo for deep, committed love.
  • Close with Tuyo/a para siempre, Con todo mi amor or Te quiero.
{{toc}}

How to start a love letter in Spanish

OpeningEnglishTone
Querido Pablo: / Querida Ana:Dear Pablo / Ana,Classic
Mi amor:My love,Warm
Mi vida:My life / my darling,Very affectionate
Amor mío:My love,Poetic
A la persona que me cambió la vida:To the person who changed my life,Dramatic

Note that, as the Real Academia Española explains, Spanish letters use a colon after the greeting, not a comma. See {{link:spanish-punctuation-rules|Spanish punctuation rules}}.

Phrases to describe your feelings

  • Desde que te conocí, mi vida es más bonita. Since I met you, my life is more beautiful.
  • Contigo me siento en casa. With you I feel at home.
  • Eres lo mejor que me ha pasado. You’re the best thing that has ever happened to me.
  • No puedo dejar de pensar en ti. I can’t stop thinking about you.
  • Me haces reír como nadie. You make me laugh like no one else.
  • Me encanta cómo me miras. I love the way you look at me.
  • Cada día te quiero más. I love you more every day.

Sharing memories

Specific memories are the heart of a good love letter:

  • ¿Te acuerdas de nuestra primera cita? Do you remember our first date?
  • Nunca olvidaré aquella tarde en la playa. I’ll never forget that afternoon on the beach.
  • Cuando me tomaste la mano por primera vez, supe que… When you took my hand for the first time, I knew that…

Notice the past tenses: the preterite for single moments (supe), the imperfect for background (hacía frío). For first-date vocabulary, see {{link:first-date-in-spanish|first date in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Talking about the future

  • Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo. I want to spend the rest of my life with you.
  • Sueño con nuestro futuro juntos. I dream of our future together.
  • Lo que más deseo es hacerte feliz. What I want most is to make you happy.
  • Contigo, cualquier lugar es mi hogar. With you, anywhere is home.
{{book:love-slowly}}

Te quiero or te amo?

Both mean “I love you”. Te quiero is warm and used with partners, family and close friends. Te amo is deeper and more solemn, usually for a committed romantic relationship, and more common in Latin America than in Spain. In a love letter, either works; te amo adds intensity. The details are in {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

How to sign off

  • Con todo mi amor, With all my love,
  • Tuyo / Tuya para siempre, Yours forever,
  • Te quiero con locura, I love you madly,
  • Siempre tuyo, Always yours,
  • Mil besos, A thousand kisses,

A sample love letter in Spanish

Mi amor:

Hoy hace un año que nos conocimos y quería escribirte algo que no fuera un mensaje rápido. ¿Te acuerdas de aquella tarde en el café, cuando se te cayó el libro y los dos nos agachamos a la vez? Todavía me río al pensarlo.

Desde entonces, mi vida es más tranquila y más bonita. Me encanta cómo cantas cuando cocinas, cómo me escuchas cuando tengo un mal día y cómo haces que todo parezca fácil. Contigo me siento en casa.

No sé qué nos traerá el futuro, pero sé que lo quiero vivir contigo. Gracias por este año precioso.

Te quiero con todo mi corazón.

Tuyo para siempre,
Daniel

In English: My love, today it’s been a year since we met… With you I feel at home… Yours forever, Daniel.

Tips for writing your own

  • Write first in simple Spanish. Short, clear sentences sound sincere.
  • Handwrite it if you can. A handwritten letter feels special in any language.
  • Don’t over-translate English idioms. “You’re my rock” doesn’t work word for word; try Eres mi apoyo. See {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}.
  • Use their name and your pet name. See {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}.

Short notes for everyday love

Not every love letter needs to be long. A note in a lunchbox or on the fridge can be just as powerful: Que tengas un día precioso. Te quiero. / Gracias por existir. / Eres mi persona favorita. / Hoy te quiero un poquito más que ayer. Short notes are perfect for practicing, too.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Querido Ana,Querida Ana:Gender agreement; colon
Eres mi roca.Eres mi apoyo / mi pilar.Idiom doesn’t transfer
Estoy enamorado con ti.Estoy enamorado de ti.Enamorarse de; conmigo/contigo
Te echo de menos mucho.Te echo mucho de menos.Natural word order
{{image:3}}

Final thoughts

The best love letter in Spanish is personal, specific and simple. Start with Mi amor, share a memory, say how they make you feel, look to the future, and sign off with all your love. For other moments in life and love, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you start a love letter in Spanish?
faq.a: With Querido/Querida + name, Mi amor, Mi vida or Amor mío, followed by a colon.

faq.q: How do you end a love letter in Spanish?
faq.a: Con todo mi amor, Tuyo/Tuya para siempre, Siempre tuyo, Mil besos or Te quiero con locura.

faq.q: Should I use te quiero or te amo in a love letter?
faq.a: Either works. Te quiero is warm and common; te amo is deeper and more solemn, especially in Latin America.
